body.x: A.I.MATICS (CEO Victor Hoon Lee) participated in the ‘Global Media Meetup’ held on July 30. Organizers arranged this meetup to inform overseas media about participating companies’ products and technologies in advance for global markets while expanding business opportunities. A.I.MATICS joined this meetup as a company submitting its AI vision inspection platform ‘AIM-T1’ for the CES 2027 Innovation Awards, with Jaewon Lee, AI LAB Specialist at A.I.MATICS, delivering the presentation on this day.

A.I.MATICS launched in 2003 as an in-house venture of Hyundai Motor Group before growing into an independent entity. Researching on-device vision AI for autonomous driving that requires immediate judgments in high-speed driving environments for over 10 years, the company secured patent-based ‘World Model AI’ and its proprietary engine ‘aimNet’. Running directly on devices without cloud dependencies, aimNet serves as a real-time AI engine that the company applied to over 520,000 vehicles, accumulating driving data equivalent to approximately 3,500 years (11 million video clips, 34 TB) alongside over 104 domestic and international patents. A.I.MATICS expands its recognition intelligence—verified in mobility—into high-volume electronics manufacturing environments where precision holds paramount importance.

body.cap: AI vision inspection platform ‘AIM-T1’ by A.I.MATICS | Image provided by A.I.MATICS

body.x: Structural challenges such as ‘reshoring’ and ‘skilled labor shortages’ lie in the background. According to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA), private investments exceeding 770 billion USD across more than 160 semiconductor projects were announced in 30 US states since 2020, while Deloitte and others project 1.9 million US manufacturing jobs to remain unfilled by 2033. While factories expand rapidly, skilled inspection personnel who guarantee quality cannot keep pace. In particular, inspection sites require over 72 hours to gather new defect datasets, manually adjust thresholds, and retrain AI models whenever products change, relying on the experience of a few skilled inspectors for micron-level pass/fail decisions. This expertise does not transfer easily to other factories.

AIM-T1 directly targets this problem. Its core patent-based ‘World Model AI’ learns object structures and surface textures in advance through self-supervised learning before seeing products, thereby generating new product inspection criteria using only 3 to 5 good reference samples without defect images. Combined with In-Context Learning and the AIM Automatic Training System (AATS), this shortened AI model transition time during New Product Introduction (NPI) from approximately 72 hours to about 4 hours. Because inspection criteria reside in software rather than hardware, even when products change, teams avoid rebuilding inspection equipment, reusing a single platform across multiple products and lines.

body.cap: A.I.MATICS AI LAB Specialist Jaewon Lee during an interview with Ubergizmo Editor-in-Chief Hubert Nguyen | Photo by AVING News

body.x: The difference from conventional methods lies in ‘what the system learns’. Rule-based systems (AOI) require humans to set thresholds, while supervised learning AI learns thousands of defect images per product, necessitating model rebuilds when products change. Conversely, AIM-T1 understands the object itself rather than a list of defects, determining flaws based on deviation from normal states to catch undefined defects. Designed for field quality engineers rather than AI experts, usage follows three simple steps: selecting good samples on-screen (Drag), confirming normal criteria formed by the system (Teach), and starting inspection (Inspect). This allows in-house quality teams—rather than external AI vendors or system integrators (SI)—to execute product switchovers directly. Hardware adopts a modular structure, adjusting camera resolution, quantity, direction, lens magnification, and lighting to fit products, applying liquid lens electronic focus stacking. Hence, it mounts directly onto existing production lines without separate inspection rooms or line redesigns.

Results emerged from real production sites. An initial version (1.0) of AIM-T1 operates on connector assembly lines at a major Korean conglomerate’s electronics production base in Vietnam, verifying up to 75,000 daily inspections, 100% detection of irregular defects, a 0.01% escape rate, and a 26% productivity boost. Catching defects as small as 10 μm, its 700 mm integrated housing operates in sync with existing line tact times. Reflecting field experiences, the company recently released its next-generation version, ‘AIM-T1 2.0’.

body.cap: Ubergizmo Editor-in-Chief Hubert Nguyen, A.I.MATICS AI LAB Specialist Jaewon Lee, and officials take a commemorative photo after concluding the Global Media Meetup. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: Market expansion accelerates in earnest as well. Currently applied to camera modules, semiconductor packages, and PCB/FPCB assembly inspections, AIM-T1 plans to expand into automotive electronic components, displays, and batteries. Using its Vietnam entity as a hub to solidify its position in Southeast Asian markets, A.I.MATICS plans step-by-step entry into North America—where semiconductor, battery, and electronics reshoring expands—and South America, centered on automotive and electronic components. To this end, the company expands collaborations with global manufacturing enterprises, automation equipment partners, and system integration firms.

Jaewon Lee, AI LAB Specialist at A.I.MATICS who delivered the presentation, stated, “Because problems differ across industries, we need industry-specialized AI rather than a single general-purpose AI.” He added, “Converting inspection expertise into software-based scalable manufacturing capabilities, we will target the global manufacturing market with an AI inspection platform that responds without retraining even when products change.”
